JUDGMENT
P. Kumararatnam, J.
The above-named Accused-Appellants (hereinafter referred to as the
Appellants) were indicted by the Attorney General in the High Court of
Colombo on the following charges namely:
Count 01 - Between 01.10.2019 and 22.10.2019, at Colombo, the 1st
Accused committed the offence of trafficking by recruiting Oksana
Karpowa Odlovina (PW01) through fraud or deception and/or by
performing any other act to bring PW 01 to Sri Lanka for the purpose of
prostitution or other forms of sexual exploitation, an offence punishable
under Section 360C(2) read with Section 360C(1)(b) of the Penal Code, as
amended by Act No. 16 of 2006.
Count 02 - At the same time period, place and during the same
transaction as mentioned in the 01st Count, the 2nd Accused-Appellant
in order to commit the offence mentioned in the 01st Count, aided and
abetted the 01st Accused-Appellant to commit the offence of trafficking
by recruiting Oksama Karpowa Odlovina (PW 01) through fraud or
deception and/or by performing any other act to bring PW 01 to Sri Lanka
for the purpose of prostitution or other forms of sexual exploitation, an

After the trial the Appellants were convicted as charged and were sentenced
as follows:
1st Appellant
First count – 07 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.25000/-
subject to a default sentence of 06 months simple imprisonment.
Third count – 07 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.25000/-
subject to a default sentence of 06 months simple imprisonment.
Fifth count – 07 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.25000/-
subject to a default sentence of 06 months simple imprisonment.
Additionally, she was ordered to pay a compensation of Rs.500,000/- with a

2nd Appellant

Being aggrieved by the aforesaid conviction and sentence, the Appellants
preferred this appeal to this court.
The Learned Counsel for the Appellants informed this court that the
Appellants have given consent to argue this matter in their absence. At the
time of argument, they were connected via the Zoom platform from the
prison.
Although the learned Counsel for the Appellants, in their written
submissions raised several grounds of appeal, at the time of argument, both
Counsel informed this court that they are only contesting the sentences
imposed in this case.
Background of the case
In this case, the Appellants are wife and husband respectively, it was alleged
that the Appellant had procured the victim for sexual activities in Sri Lanka.
The victim, PW1, is a Russian National and had come to Sri Lanka several
times and worked in shops before she had gotten to know the 1st Appellant.
The 1st Appellant had brought her back to Sri Lanka and had procured her
for sexual activities until the 1st Appellant was sentenced to jail. After the 1st
Appellant was jailed, the 2nd Appellant had continued to procure the victim
for sexual activities until she lodged her complaint with the Tourist Police.
6 | P a g e
The victim had visited Sri Lanka on five occasions prior to 2019, which was
confirmed by the Department of Immigration and Emigration. The victim had
become acquainted with the 1st Appellant via Facebook and had thereafter
come to Sri Lanka on 22.10.2019 using an air ticket sent by the 1st Appellant.
Upon her arrival to Sri Lanka, she was engaged in prostitution by PW1. This
was continued by the 1st Appellant until late January 2020. Thereafter, the
2nd Appellant had continued the same until March 2021. When she asked
for money from the 2nd Appellant to purchase an air ticket to return to her
country, the 2nd Appellant had refused to give money to her. As a result, she
had lodged her first complaint at the Sri Lanka Tourist Police in Colpetty
regarding a dispute over money in the month of March 2021 and had left the
accommodation provided at the Peterson Lane. The victim had not
mentioned about the procuration by the Appellants to the police. In her
second statement given in May 2021 too, she had not mentioned about the
procuration by the Appellants to the police.
In the meantime, a person called Rameez had taken her to Trincomalee and
assaulted her. She had lodged a complaint at the Trincomalee Police
regarding this incident but had not disclosed that she was used for
prostitution by the Appellants.
After coming to Colombo, she had rented a room at Roadster Studio,
Torrington, Colombo. At that time, a complaint was lodged by the IOM
regarding her detention at the Roadster Hotel and the CID had commenced
investigation and arrested the Appellants and filed the indictment in the High
Court of Colombo.
The JMO and the Consultant Physician both had not conducted a proper
physical examination but had submitted a report that the victim was
suffering from severe depression and post-traumatic stress disorder.
7 | P a g e
Both Counsel had strenuously argued that the Learned High Court Judge
has failed to consider the sentencing submissions made on behalf of the
Appellants.
As stated above, the Appellants are wife and husband and have children.
According to the submissions made before the High Court it was brought to
the attention of the Court that the 1st Appellant had married previously and
had two male children. One child, was 17 years old and the other child was
15 years old at the time of sentencing. The elder son had gone back to
Uzbekistan and the younger child had been admitted to the Bandaragama
Child Care Centre, where he is presently residing.
Upon the present marriage, she had delivered a female child who was 07
years of age at the time of sentencing and she too had been admitted to a
child care home given the present situation. The 2nd Appellant was a three-
wheeler driver and is the sole breadwinner of his family. He bore the
responsibility of looking after his mother and sister who was an
undergraduate at a university. Both the Counsel submitted that their
children are suffering due to their incarceration and therefore seeks the
mercy of this court to re-consider the sentence only to re-unite with their
children.
The learned Deputy Solicitor General in keeping with the highest traditions
of the Attorney General’s Department too agreed that this is an appropriate
case to re-consider the sentence imposed by the Learned High Court Judge
in considering the vulnerable situation of the children of the Appellants.
After the conviction of an Accused person, the discretion in imposing the
relevant sentence would lie with that particular Court, while being guided by
a number of factors, such as the circumstances under which the offence was
committed by the Accused. Where such specific sentencing guidelines would
not be available, it would be necessary to discuss the principles that must
be followed when imposing sentences.
8 | P a g e
In the case of The Attorney General v H.N.de Silva 57 NLR 121 Per
BASNAYAKE, A.C.J.-
" A Judge should, in determining the proper sentence, first consider the
gravity of the offence as it appears from the nature of the act itself and
should have regard to the punishment provided in the Penal Code or other
statute under which the offender is charged. He should also regard the
effect of the punishment as a deterrent and consider to what extent it will
be effective. If the offender held a position of trust or belonged to a service
which enjoys the public confidence that must be taken into account in
assessing the punishment. The incidence of crimes of the nature of which
the offender has been found to be guilty and the difficulty of detection are
also matters which should receive due consideration. The reformation of
the criminal, though no doubt an important consideration, is subordinate
to the others I have mentioned. Where the public interest or the welfare of
the State (which are synonymous) outweighs the previous good character,
antecedents and age of the offender, public interest must prevail. "
In the case of Don Percy Nanayakkara v The Republic of Sri Lanka [1993]
1 SLR 71 the Court held that:
“In assessing punishment, the Court has to consider the matter from the
point of both the offender and the public. The accused had held high public
office and exercised extensive statutory power in conducting public
examinations in this country. These examinations have to be conducted
fairly and the results declared accurately. Thousands of students who face
public examinations, every year, should have complete confidence in the
fairness and accuracy of every process of the examinations. The accused
has subverted the very basis of this confidence by his conduct in
dishonestly showing favour to persons with whom he was acquainted.
9 | P a g e
Therefore, public interest demands that he should be imposed a deterrent
punishment.”
In the case of Asan Mohammed Rizwan v Attorney General, CA [PHC] APN
141/2013 decided on March 25, 2015 it was held:
“Sentencing is an important aspect in the administration of criminal
justice system. A sentence ranges from death penalty to the mere
censure in the form of good behavior bond or probation. There are
multiple considerations relevant to the determination of a sentence. The
most important consideration is the seriousness of the crime.
Jurisprudentially, this position is persuasive despite pragmatic
difficulties associated with matching the harshness of the sanction to
the severity of the crime.
The judges are to pass lawful and appropriate sentence upon the
accused being convicted. In doing so, judges are to address their minds
to the objective of sentencing particularly when exercising the discretion
given to them under the law. Then only a correct sentence could be
passed upon a convicted accused. If not, criticism on lack of uniformity,
consistency and transparency in imposing sentences are bound to
surface. Therefore, it is necessary for the judges to keep in mind the
objectives of sentencing and also the sentencing guidelines, in order to
arrive at the correct and appropriate decision.
Objectives of sentencing include the following:
(i) To punish offenders to an extent and in a manner, which is
just in all the circumstances;
(ii) To protect the community from offender;
(iii) To deter offenders or other persons from committing offences
of the same or similar nature;
10 | P a g e
(iv) To establish conditions so that rehabilitation of offenders may
be promoted or facilitated;
(v) To signify that the court and the community denounce the
commission of such offences;
(vi) To maintain the required standards of societal expectations in
making decisions;
(vii) To prevent overcrowding prisons also could be considered as
one such objective particularly when it comes to developing
countries such as ours.”
In the case of Bandage Sumindra Jayanthi v. Attorney General (2015) 1
SLR 20 it was held:
“Sentencing belongs to the domain of the trial judge but that is no ground
for the prosecuting counsel to be complacent about his role in responding
to the mitigatory plea of a defense counsel.”
Under Section 360C of the Penal Code as amended, the minimum sentence
is 2 years imprisonment of either description and the maximum sentence is
20 years imprisonment of either description.
Under Section 360A of the Penal Code as amended, the minimum sentence
is 2 years imprisonment of either description and the maximum sentence is
10 years imprisonment of either description.
The Learned High Court Judge had imposed 07 years rigorous imprisonment
on each of the counts they had been charged subject to each sentence
running concurrently.
Considering all the circumstances with special attention to their children, I
consider imposing 4 years rigorous imprisonment is appropriate in this case.
Hence, their sentence on each count is reduced to 4 years rigorous
11 | P a g e
imprisonment which will run concurrently. Hence, each Appellant will have
to serve 04 years rigorous imprisonment. The fine and the compensation
imposed by the Learned High Court Judge will remain the same.
Considering the fact that the Appellants have been in remand custody since
their sentence, I order their sentences to take effect from the date of
conviction, namely 10.12.2024.
The Appeal is dismissed subject to the variation in the prison sentence.
The Registrar is directed to send this judgment to the High Court of Colombo
along with the original case record.
